title: CORS preflight behavior · Choosing HTTP success and failure statuses

blocks.text: For some cross-origin calls, the browser asks permission before sending the intended method and headers.
An OPTIONS preflight asks whether an intended method and headers are permitted. Not every cross-origin request is preflighted.

Include Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method; include Access-Control-Request-Headers when applicable. Compare the caller’s origin, method and headers with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers. A credentialed response needs an explicit allowed origin, not *, plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.

blocks.text: Compare the supplied OPTIONS exchange: its caller origin, intended PUT and requested content-type must align with the corresponding allow headers. The actual PUT is a separate conditional next step, not completed by OPTIONS. For a credentialed response, check both the explicit allowed origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
Only some cross-origin requests are preflighted. A wildcard allowed origin is not the required response for a credentialed exchange.

steps.eyebrow: Choosing HTTP success and failure statuses
steps.title: Establish the rule

blocks.text: Order creation, an absent target and unexpected failure need distinct HTTP outcomes.
The classes are informational 1xx, successful 2xx, redirection 3xx, client error 4xx and server error 5xx.

Use 200 for success, 201 for resource creation and 204 for success without response content. 400 means a perceived request error; 401 lacks valid authentication credentials; 403 refuses fulfillment; 404 does not find or disclose the target; 409 conflicts with current state. 500 denotes an unexpected server condition; 503 temporary inability, such as overload or maintenance.

steps.eyebrow: Choosing HTTP success and failure statuses
steps.title: Why the distinction matters

blocks.text: Choose the outcome class, then its specific meaning. Retrieval differs from creation; missing valid credentials differ from refusal; conflict differs from a target not found or disclosed. Unexpected failure differs from temporary inability. Producing a JSON body does not itself justify a successful status.

steps.eyebrow: Choosing HTTP success and failure statuses
steps.title: Reason through an example

blocks.text: Use the orders outcome table: retrieval 200, creation 201, no-content success 204. Compare 400 request error, 401 missing valid credentials, 403 refusal, 404 target not found or disclosed and 409 current-state conflict. Unexpected server failure is 500; temporary inability is 503. These meanings do not promise automatic framework behavior.
Client and server errors are different classes. A 204 success has no response content.

public.prompt: Replace the zero value in each supplied variable with the status appropriate for its named outcome. The outcomes are: order_retrieval_status = retrieval; order_creation_status = creation; order_no_content_status = no content; order_request_error_status = request error; order_missing_credentials_status = missing credentials; order_refusal_status = refusal; order_not_found_status = not found; order_conflict_status = conflict; order_unexpected_failure_status = unexpected failure; order_temporary_unavailability_status = temporary unavailability. Keep the variable names and inspection helper unchanged. The checker grades every assignment; no endpoint implementation is needed. Also label each # STATUS_CLASS pattern as informational, successful, redirection, client error or server error. Each class comment is graded. In this supplied comment-source editor, Python source lines have a # PY prefix. Keep that prefix and edit the requested code after it; the unchanged compiler executes those lines. Lines belonging to the supplied checker are scaffolding, not new syntax to learn.
